Chapter 2. The Lies That Take Root and How They Grow.
You know, it’s kind of wild how much power a single thought can have. Maybe it starts as something small—like, “I’m not as talented as everyone else.” At first, it’s just a passing idea. But if you don’t catch it, that little thought can quietly turn into a belief that shapes how you see yourself for years.
These beliefs rarely show up all at once. They grow slowly, almost like weeds, getting stronger every time they’re repeated or “proven” by experience.
Let me give you an example. Imagine a woman who goes through a tough breakup. At first, it hurts—naturally. But soon, she starts telling herself, “Maybe I’m just unlovable.” Suddenly, the end of her relationship isn’t just a sad event—it’s evidence that something’s wrong with her. Every time she sees a happy couple, that feeling just grows. She pulls away from others, convinced that nobody would want her anyway. That lie, once planted, really digs in.
Or take someone in a high-pressure job. One mistake, and she starts to believe she’s not good enough. So, she works extra hours, trying to fix things, but the anxiety only gets worse. The harder she tries, the more that fear of failure feels like the truth.
The thing is, these patterns are so common. Most of us are carrying around a handful of these lies—picked up from family, from our culture, or from tough moments that just didn’t go the way we hoped. Maybe you’ve heard messages like, “People like us don’t do that,” or you’ve seen impossible standards everywhere you look. Sometimes, it’s just the sting of disappointment that plants the seed.
What makes these lies so sneaky is how quiet they are. They don’t announce themselves with a big warning. Instead, they slip in as background assumptions—like, “I’ll never change,” or, “Maybe I don’t deserve to be happy.” Over time, these thoughts become so familiar, we stop questioning them. They’re just the soundtrack playing quietly in the background.
But even if they’re quiet, their effects are real. They change the way we approach relationships, our jobs, even our sense of purpose. They can lead to self-sabotage, missed chances, and always feeling like we’re not quite enough. For some people, these beliefs get so deeply rooted that it’s hard to imagine life without them.
But here’s the good news—there’s a way out. The first step is simply noticing the lies. It takes honesty, and it’s not always comfortable. You’ve got to ask yourself some tough questions: Where did this belief come from? Is it really true, or just something you picked up along the way? What’s the real evidence?
And yeah, it can feel awkward—almost like pulling weeds that have been growing for years. But as you start calling out these lies for what they are, they lose their hold. Most people find that these beliefs aren’t set in stone. They’re not facts—they’re stories. And the best part? Stories can be rewritten.
